### case_derived_1480: Anticipatory Bail — Section 482 BNSS — Conditions, Cancellation and White Collar Offences *(Two-track · Criminal · Bail Law · Sessions Court/High Court)*

**Round 1**

*Junior Advocate:* Our client — a senior bank official — apprehends arrest in a bank fraud case. We want to apply for anticipatory bail under Section 482 BNSS. What are the factors the court considers?

*Decision dimension targeted:* Identifying the factors governing the grant of anticipatory bail under Section 482 BNSS and the special considerations in white-collar financial fraud cases.
*Why this question wins:* Anticipatory bail in economic offence cases has a specific jurisprudence — courts apply a higher standard than in ordinary cases; the student must know this differential treatment.
*Plausible bad alternative:* Applying the same standard as for anticipatory bail in ordinary criminal cases.
*Why bad alternative loses:* The Supreme Court has consistently held that economic offences and financial frauds are treated more stringently than ordinary crimes — courts are reluctant to grant anticipatory bail where the fraud is of magnitude; treating them identically ignores settled jurisprudence.

*Senior Advocate:* Section 482 BNSS (formerly Section 438 CrPC) empowers the Sessions Court or High Court to grant anticipatory bail — a direction that in the event of arrest, the person shall be released on bail. The factors under Section 482(1) include: (a) nature and gravity of accusation; (b) antecedents of the applicant; (c) possibility of the applicant fleeing justice; (d) whether the accusation appears to be made for humiliating or injuring the applicant. For white-collar bank fraud cases, the Supreme Court in *P. Chidambaram v. CBI* (2019) 9 SCC 24 held that the gravity of economic offences is relevant — elaborate fraud cases where money has moved through multiple accounts and the accused may have concealed evidence or could influence witnesses deserve more scrutiny. We pre-empt these concerns: (a) our client has deep roots in the jurisdiction — family, business, property; (b) is willing to surrender the passport and cooperate with investigation; (c) the allegation has not been independently verified — the FIR is based on a complaint without forensic analysis; (d) there is no prima facie evidence linking our client to the fraudulent accounts.

**Round 2**

*Junior Advocate:* The court wants to impose conditions on anticipatory bail — one condition proposed is that our client appear for interrogation whenever summoned. Is this a permissible condition?

*Decision dimension targeted:* The scope of conditions that can be imposed on anticipatory bail under Section 482(2) BNSS and the limits of permissible conditions.
*Why this question wins:* Conditions on anticipatory bail must strike a balance between investigation facilitation and individual liberty — understanding permissible and impermissible conditions is practically essential.
*Plausible bad alternative:* Accepting all conditions proposed by the prosecution without challenge.
*Why bad alternative loses:* Some conditions — like unlimited custodial interrogation even under bail — effectively negate the anticipatory bail; counsel must challenge unreasonable conditions that render the bail illusory.

*Senior Advocate:* Section 482(2) BNSS permits the court to impose conditions including: (a) a condition that the person makes himself available for interrogation by the police officer as and when required; (b) that the person does not leave India without prior permission; (c) that the person surrenders the passport; (d) that the person does not tamper with evidence or contact prosecution witnesses. The condition of appearing for interrogation when required is expressly permitted and is a standard condition — we accept it. However, the Supreme Court in *Gurbaksh Singh Sibbia v. State of Punjab* (1980) 2 SCC 565 held that anticipatory bail cannot be limited to a fixed period — it must continue until the bail is cancelled. We resist any condition that: (a) imposes custodial interrogation — once bail is granted, investigation must be through Section 61 BNSS summons, not arrest; (b) restricts travel without notice rather than without permission — a blanket travel ban may be disproportionate; (c) requires surrender to custody on any occasion — this would negate the anticipatory bail itself. We specifically resist conditions that effectively allow re-arrest without cancellation of bail.

**Round 3**

*Junior Advocate:* The CBI now applies for cancellation of the anticipatory bail on the ground that the accused refused to answer questions during interrogation by claiming his right against self-incrimination. Is this a valid ground for cancellation?

*Decision dimension targeted:* Whether exercise of the right against self-incrimination during interrogation under anticipatory bail constitutes a breach of conditions justifying cancellation.
*Why this question wins:* This is a sophisticated constitutional-procedural question at the intersection of bail conditions and fundamental rights — the student must understand that asserting a constitutional right cannot be punished by bail cancellation.
*Plausible bad alternative:* Conceding that the client breached the "cooperation" condition by refusing to answer.
*Why bad alternative loses:* The right against self-incrimination under Article 20(3) is a fundamental right — it cannot be waived as a condition of bail; conceding that its exercise constitutes a bail breach surrenders a constitutional right for liberty.

*Senior Advocate:* Article 20(3) of the Constitution provides that no person accused of any offence shall be compelled to be a witness against himself. This is an inviolable fundamental right — it cannot be contractually waived, and it cannot be made a condition of bail. A bail condition that requires the accused to answer all questions during interrogation would, if interpreted as requiring incriminating disclosures, be unconstitutional as a compelled waiver of Article 20(3). The Supreme Court in *Nandini Satpathy v. P.L. Dani* (1978) 2 SCC 424 held that the right extends to police interrogation — the accused cannot be compelled to answer questions whose answers would incriminate him. The "cooperation" condition in anticipatory bail means cooperation with the process — attending interrogation, providing documents, not fleeing — it does not mean surrendering the right to silence on incriminating questions. The CBI's application for cancellation on this ground is misconceived — we oppose it robustly on Article 20(3) grounds. Bail can be cancelled for breach of conditions or for new material showing danger of flight or evidence tampering — not for exercise of a constitutional right.


### case_derived_1481: Companies Act 2013 — Section 241/242 — Oppression and Mismanagement in Closely Held Companies *(Two-track · Commercial · Company Law · NCLT)*

**Round 1**

*Junior Advocate:* Our client holds 30% shares in a private limited company. The majority shareholders (70%) have been taking major decisions — including diverting company funds to a related party — without calling Board or general meetings as required by the Companies Act. We want to file a petition under Section 241. What must we establish?

*Decision dimension targeted:* Understanding the locus standi requirements and substantive grounds for a petition under Sections 241-242 of the Companies Act 2013.
*Why this question wins:* Oppression and mismanagement petitions under Sections 241-242 have specific threshold conditions — the student must know who can file, when, and on what grounds.
*Plausible bad alternative:* Advising the client to file a civil suit for breach of fiduciary duty by directors.
*Why bad alternative loses:* A civil suit is an available remedy but does not provide the range of corporate remedies — change of management, winding up, buyout — that Sections 241-242 uniquely offer; advising only the civil suit underserves the client.

*Senior Advocate:* For a petition under Section 241 of the Companies Act 2013, our client must first establish locus standi. Section 244 specifies the eligibility conditions: in the case of a company having a share capital, the application can be made by at least 100 members or 10% of the total members, whichever is less, or members holding at least 10% of the issued share capital. Our client holds 30% — he clearly meets the threshold. On the substantive grounds: Section 241(1) permits a member to apply to the NCLT if the affairs of the company have been or are being conducted in a manner prejudicial to the public interest or prejudicial or oppressive to the member(s) or prejudicial to the interests of the company. "Oppressive conduct" under the historic *Needle Industries India Ltd. v. Needle Industries Newey Ltd.* (1981) 3 SCC 333 framework means conduct that is burdensome, harsh, and wrongful — a conscious squeeze-out of the minority. The diversion of funds to a related party without disclosure or Board approval is a classic oppression and mismanagement scenario.

**Round 2**

*Junior Advocate:* The majority shareholders argue that they are in the majority and have the right to conduct the company as they see fit. Is there a doctrine that protects the majority's decision-making autonomy?

*Decision dimension targeted:* The tension between the majority rule principle (Foss v. Harbottle) and the minority shareholder's protection under Sections 241-242.
*Why this question wins:* Understanding Foss v. Harbottle and its exceptions is foundational for any oppression and mismanagement petition — the majority rule is the defence and the student must know the exceptions that defeat it.
*Plausible bad alternative:* Ignoring the majority rule doctrine and proceeding as if the minority's grievance automatically trumps it.
*Why bad alternative loses:* Courts do apply Foss v. Harbottle as a threshold matter — if the grievance can be ratified by the majority, it is an internal company matter; the student must engage with the exceptions to establish that ratification is not available here.

*Senior Advocate:* The rule in *Foss v. Harbottle* (1843) 2 Hare 461 holds that the proper plaintiff in a wrong done to the company is the company itself — the majority decides whether to sue. This protects majoritarian autonomy. However, the Indian courts and Parliament have recognised well-established exceptions: (a) acts that are illegal or ultra vires the company and cannot be ratified even by the majority; (b) acts that constitute a fraud on the minority — where the majority benefit at the expense of the minority and control the voting to prevent action; (c) acts that require a qualified majority for their approval — here, certain Related Party Transactions under Section 188 require special resolution or Board approval with interested directors absent from the vote. The diversion of funds to a majority shareholder's related entity is exactly the fraud on the minority exception: the majority cannot ratify their own fraud. We establish that the Related Party Transaction was not approved per Section 188 procedure and that the majority directly benefited — this falls within the fraud exception and the NCLT has jurisdiction.

**Round 3**

*Junior Advocate:* What remedies can the NCLT grant if it finds oppression and mismanagement?

*Decision dimension targeted:* The range of remedies available under Section 242 of the Companies Act 2013 and the most commonly sought remedies in minority oppression cases.
*Why this question wins:* The breadth and creativity of remedies available under Section 242 is what makes the petition powerful — the student must know the range beyond just "winding up."
*Plausible bad alternative:* Advising that the only remedy for oppression is winding up of the company.
*Why bad alternative loses:* Winding up is explicitly the last resort — Section 242(3) says the NCLT shall not wind up the company if other appropriate relief is available; advising winding up as the primary remedy would be resisted and is factually incorrect about the legislative intent.

*Senior Advocate:* Section 242 of the Companies Act 2013 grants the NCLT a wide range of remedies — the power to make any order as it thinks fit to bring to an end the matters complained of. The most commonly sought and granted remedies include: (a) buyout order — directing the majority to buy out the minority shareholder at a fair value determined by an independent valuer, which is often the most commercially practical remedy; (b) change of management — removing the oppressive directors and appointing new ones; (c) modification or setting aside of the impugned transactions — directing the company to recover the diverted funds from the related party; (d) restriction on transfer of shares by the majority to prevent further manipulation; (e) winding up — as a last resort where the relationship between shareholders has broken down irretrievably. In our case, we pray primarily for: (a) setting aside the related party transactions and recovering the diverted funds; (b) a fair buyout of our client's 30% at independently valued price; or alternatively (c) a Board restructuring with independent directors to prevent further misconduct. The NCLT has held consistently that the winding up prayer is a backstop — the primary focus is on preserving the company while protecting the minority.

---

### case_derived_1482: Article 311 — Dismissal of Government Servant — Major Penalty and Departmental Enquiry *(Two-track · Service · Administrative Law · High Court)*

**Round 1**

*Junior Advocate:* Our client, a Class I government officer, has been dismissed from service following a departmental inquiry. The inquiry officer found him guilty of financial irregularity. We want to challenge the dismissal. What is the constitutional framework for protection?

*Decision dimension targeted:* Understanding the Article 311(2) procedural protections for civil servants facing dismissal and the stages at which challenge is available.
*Why this question wins:* Article 311 is the constitutional guarantee for government servants — the student must know its specific requirements, which the government frequently violates.
*Plausible bad alternative:* Advising the client to file an appeal before the appellate authority only, without challenging the constitutionality of the procedure.
*Why bad alternative loses:* If the procedure itself violated Article 311, the entire enquiry is a nullity — statutory appeal remedies cannot cure a constitutional invalidity; the constitutional challenge must be independently pursued.

*Senior Advocate:* Article 311(2) of the Constitution provides that no civil servant shall be dismissed or removed or reduced in rank except after an inquiry in which he has been informed of the charges against him and given a reasonable opportunity of being heard in respect of those charges. This creates three mandatory safeguards: (a) a charge sheet specifying the charges in sufficient detail for the officer to understand and respond; (b) an opportunity to take assistance of a defence representative (though not necessarily a lawyer — subject to the relevant service rules); (c) a written findings and reasoned order after the inquiry. We examine the departmental inquiry record for violations: Was the charge sheet specific enough? Was the officer given opportunity to cross-examine the witnesses against him? Was the inquiry officer an appropriate officer — not a subordinate of the charged officer's superior? Was the Presenting Officer's closing statement shown to the accused for rebuttal? Any significant violation of these procedural guarantees renders the inquiry order void and the dismissal unconstitutional.

**Round 2**

*Junior Advocate:* The inquiry officer's report was not furnished to our client before the dismissal order was passed. The disciplinary authority reviewed the report and passed the dismissal order without giving our client an opportunity to respond to the inquiry report. Is this a violation of Article 311?

*Decision dimension targeted:* The second show cause notice requirement — whether the charged officer must be given an opportunity to respond to the Inquiry Officer's adverse findings before the dismissal order is passed.
*Why this question wins:* The second show cause notice requirement is one of the most litigated procedural points in service law — the Supreme Court's position has evolved and the student must know the current law.
*Plausible bad alternative:* Assuming there is no requirement to provide the inquiry report to the employee before passing the final order.
*Why bad alternative loses:* The Supreme Court has specifically held that the employee must be given an opportunity to respond to the inquiry officer's findings before the punishment order is passed — the requirement flows from the principles of natural justice even if not expressly mandated by Article 311.

*Senior Advocate:* The Supreme Court in *Union of India v. Mohd. Ramzan Khan* (1991) 1 SCC 588 (five-judge bench) held that furnishing a copy of the inquiry officer's report to the delinquent officer before passing the final order of punishment is mandatory under Article 311(2) read with the principles of natural justice — it is required to enable the officer to make an effective representation against the punishment proposed. In *Managing Director ECIL v. B. Karunakar* (1993) 4 SCC 727 (seven-judge bench), the Supreme Court refined this and held that failure to supply the inquiry report to the employee before the punishment order vitiates the order — but the appropriate remedy is not necessarily acquittal; the authority must supply the report and give the employee an opportunity to respond, and then pass a fresh order. If the defect is cured by showing the report before the punishment order, no violation exists. In our case, the report was not furnished at any stage before dismissal — this is a clear violation and the dismissal order is constitutionally infirm. We file a writ before the High Court under Article 226 for a declaration of invalidity and reinstatement with back wages.

**Round 3**

*Junior Advocate:* The Government argues that even if there was a procedural defect, the officer was genuinely guilty of misconduct and the dismissal should not be set aside. Can the court uphold dismissal despite procedural violations?

*Decision dimension targeted:* The consequence of procedural violations in departmental enquiries — whether courts can validate punishment despite procedural infirmity.
*Why this question wins:* Courts are sometimes sympathetic to the "no prejudice" argument — the student must know when procedural violations are curable and when they are not.
*Plausible bad alternative:* Accepting that if guilt is clear, procedural violations are immaterial.
*Why bad alternative loses:* This fundamentally undermines Article 311 — the guarantee of fair procedure is not conditional on the officer's ultimate guilt; procedure and substance operate independently.

*Senior Advocate:* The Supreme Court has been clear: procedural violations in departmental enquiries are not validated by substantive guilt. In *B. Karunakar* (1993) the Court held that denial of the inquiry report causes prejudice presumptively — the officer was denied the opportunity to demonstrate that the findings were erroneous or that the punishment is disproportionate. The prejudice is not merely to the officer's innocent plea — it is to his ability to respond to an adverse finding. The court cannot substitute its own assessment of guilt for the procedural safeguards Parliament and the Constitution guarantee. The remedy in *B. Karunakar* is remand — the authority must supply the report, hear the officer, and pass a fresh order. If the fresh order is also dismissal, the government can still dismiss — but the procedure must be followed. We do not argue that our client is innocent at the writ stage — we argue that the procedure was violated, the dismissal is void, and the authority must start fresh from the point of supply of the inquiry report. Any back wages during the period of wrongful dismissal (pending reinstatement and fresh enquiry) is also claimable.


### case_derived_1483: Consumer Protection Act 2019 — Deficiency in Banking Services — Interest on Delayed FD Renewal *(Two-track · Consumer · Banking Services · District Commission)*

**Round 1**

*Junior Advocate:* Our client invested Rs. 5 lakh in a Fixed Deposit with a nationalised bank. The bank failed to auto-renew the FD on maturity and the amount remained idle for six months without any interest. The client now claims compensation for the lost interest. Can he approach the Consumer Forum?

*Decision dimension targeted:* Establishing that banking services constitute a "service" under the Consumer Protection Act 2019 and that the bank's failure to renew is a "deficiency in service."
*Why this question wins:* The threshold questions — whether the bank is a "service provider" and whether failure to auto-renew is a "deficiency" — must be established before any claim can proceed.
*Plausible bad alternative:* Filing a civil suit for breach of contract against the bank.
*Why bad alternative loses:* While a civil suit is available, Consumer Forums offer faster, cheaper and equally binding relief with power to award compensation and costs — not advising the Consumer Forum option when it is clearly applicable fails the client.

*Senior Advocate:* Banking services are explicitly covered as "services" under Section 2(42) of the Consumer Protection Act 2019. A person who avails of banking services — including deposit services — is a "consumer" under Section 2(7). A nationalised bank is a "service provider." Deficiency in service under Section 2(11) is defined as any fault, imperfection, shortcoming or inadequacy in the quality, nature and manner of performance as required under any law for the time being in force or under any contract, or as is expected by the consumer. The bank's failure to auto-renew a Fixed Deposit as per the agreed terms of the FD contract — or the bank's own policy — is a deficiency in service. The six months of idle period without interest represents the quantifiable financial loss caused by this deficiency. We file a complaint before the District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission under Section 35 of the CPA 2019 claiming: (a) the interest on the FD for the six-month idle period at the contracted FD rate; (b) compensation for the mental agony and inconvenience caused; (c) costs of litigation.

**Round 2**

*Junior Advocate:* The bank argues that the FD was an "investment" and investment services are outside the Consumer Forum's jurisdiction. Is this correct?

*Decision dimension targeted:* Distinguishing between investment services (outside consumer jurisdiction) and banking deposit services (within jurisdiction).
*Why this question wins:* The "investment vs. service" distinction is a common bank defence in Consumer Forums — the student must know the applicable jurisprudence.
*Plausible bad alternative:* Accepting that all financial products are "investments" outside Consumer Forum jurisdiction.
*Why bad alternative loses:* This sweeping argument conflates all financial products — the courts have specifically held that Fixed Deposits with banks are banking services, not "investments" in the securities law sense; accepting the argument without challenge concedes a valid claim.

*Senior Advocate:* The bank's argument conflates two different categories. "Investment" activities excluded from consumer protection typically refer to securities trading, mutual funds, and similar market-linked instruments where the consumer bears market risk and the service provider merely facilitates the transaction. A Fixed Deposit with a bank is a banking service — the bank is obligated to repay principal and interest at a contracted rate; there is no market risk borne by the depositor. The National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission in numerous decisions — including *LIC v. Consumer Education & Research Society* and *Oriental Bank of Commerce v. Smt. Savita* — has held that banking services including FD-related services are squarely within the Consumer Forum's jurisdiction. The bank is not merely an investment adviser — it is the service provider that accepted the deposit and contracted to provide the FD service. Its failure to renew is a service deficiency, not an investment risk.

**Round 3**

*Junior Advocate:* Our client also suffered because the bank delayed releasing a fixed deposit prematurely when he urgently needed funds for a medical emergency. Can he claim compensation for the medical consequences of the delay?

*Decision dimension targeted:* The scope of compensation for consequential loss in consumer disputes and the standard for awarding compensation beyond the direct financial loss.
*Why this question wins:* Consequential compensation in consumer disputes — beyond the direct loss — is available but governed by specific principles; the student must know what can and cannot be claimed.
*Plausible bad alternative:* Advising that consumer forums can only award direct financial loss, not consequential damages.
*Why bad alternative loses:* Section 39(1)(d) of the CPA 2019 specifically allows District Commissions to award compensation for injury, loss or suffering suffered by the consumer — this includes consequential damages; limiting to only direct financial loss understates the remedy.

*Senior Advocate:* Section 39(1) of the Consumer Protection Act 2019 empowers the Consumer Commission to direct payment of compensation to the consumer for any loss or injury suffered as a result of the deficiency in service. The Supreme Court in *Ghaziabad Development Authority v. Balbir Singh* (2004) 5 SCC 65 held that compensation in consumer cases should be commensurate with the loss suffered — it can include consequential loss if it flows naturally from the deficiency. If the bank's delay in releasing the FD directly caused our client to be unable to pay for timely medical treatment, and the medical consequences are documented — delayed treatment, worsening of condition, additional medical expenses — these are consequential losses that can be awarded. We must document carefully: (a) the client's urgent request for premature withdrawal on a specific date; (b) the bank's refusal or delay; (c) the medical emergency and the financial need; (d) the medical records showing the treatment delayed and any consequences. The causal link between the bank's deficiency and the medical consequences must be clearly established — this is the key to awarding consequential compensation rather than merely the interest loss.

---

### case_derived_1484: Double Taxation — Section 90 Income Tax Act — DTAA Override and Resident vs. Non-Resident Status *(Two-track · Revenue · International Tax · ITAT/High Court)*

**Round 1**

*Junior Advocate:* Our client is an Indian-origin professional who has been working in the UAE for seven years and files tax returns in the UAE. The Indian Income Tax Department claims he is a resident of India — based on his passport travel records showing he spent more than 182 days in India in a particular year — and wants to tax his global income. What is the residency analysis?

*Decision dimension targeted:* Applying the Section 6 Income Tax Act residency test and the tie-breaker rules in the India-UAE DTAA to determine tax residency.
*Why this question wins:* Residency determination is the foundational step in international tax — getting it wrong makes the subsequent DTAA analysis irrelevant.
*Plausible bad alternative:* Arguing that an Indian-origin person living abroad can never be a tax resident of India.
*Why bad alternative loses:* Origin has nothing to do with tax residency — residency is purely a function of physical presence and residential status tests under Section 6 ITA; asserting origin as a defence is legally wrong.

*Senior Advocate:* Under Section 6(1) of the Income Tax Act 1961, an individual is a resident of India if he is in India for 182 days or more during the relevant financial year. If this threshold is met, our client is a resident for that year under the domestic law — and as a resident, his global income is taxable. However, the India-UAE DTAA (a comprehensive tax treaty) contains tie-breaker rules that apply when both India and the UAE regard the individual as a resident. If the UAE also considers him a resident (UAE has a tax residency certificate regime), we apply the DTAA Article on "Residence" — typically a sequential tie-breaker: (a) permanent home — does he have a permanent home in India, or only in UAE? (b) centre of vital interests — family, social, economic ties; (c) habitual abode — which country does he spend more time in habitually? (d) nationality. If the tie-breaker points to UAE, he is treated as a UAE resident for DTAA purposes and India can only tax Indian-sourced income — not global income. We obtain a UAE Tax Residency Certificate and apply the DTAA.

**Round 2**

*Junior Advocate:* The AO argues that the India-UAE DTAA does not apply because the UAE does not levy income tax and therefore there is no "double taxation" to relieve. Is this a valid objection?

*Decision dimension targeted:* Whether a DTAA can be invoked when one country imposes no tax, and the Indian law's position on this.
*Why this question wins:* The "no double taxation if one country has no tax" argument is made by the Revenue in UAE and similar cases — the student must know why this argument fails.
*Plausible bad alternative:* Accepting that the DTAA is inapplicable because the UAE has no income tax.
*Why bad alternative loses:* The Supreme Court in *Azadi Bachao Andolan v. Union of India* (2004) 10 SCC 1 upheld the India-Mauritius DTAA even though Mauritius imposed virtually no tax; the principle that a DTAA need not be invoked only to relieve actual double taxation — it also allocates taxing rights — is settled law.

*Senior Advocate:* The AO's argument has been specifically rejected by the Indian courts. In *Azadi Bachao Andolan v. Union of India* (2004) 10 SCC 1, the Supreme Court upheld that a DTAA can be invoked even if one country does not actually impose tax — the treaty allocates taxing rights and provides exemptions independent of whether actual double taxation occurs. The UAE's lack of income tax is irrelevant to the treaty's applicability — what matters is whether the UAE is a "contracting state" under the DTAA (yes) and whether the taxpayer is a "resident of a contracting state" within the meaning of the treaty (determined by the tie-breaker). Once our client is determined to be a UAE resident under the DTAA tie-breaker, the India-UAE DTAA allocates to India the right to tax only Indian-sourced income. The AO cannot ignore the DTAA — Section 90(2) of the Income Tax Act expressly provides that wherever a DTAA exists, the taxpayer can choose to be governed by whichever of the domestic law or DTAA provisions is more beneficial. The DTAA is more beneficial here — we elect it.

**Round 3**

*Junior Advocate:* Even if the client is a UAE resident under the DTAA, the AO is proposing to deny DTAA benefits citing the Principal Purpose Test (PPT) introduced through the Multilateral Instrument (MLI). Is the PPT applicable to the India-UAE DTAA?

*Decision dimension targeted:* Understanding the MLI's modification of bilateral DTAAs through the PPT and its applicability to the India-UAE treaty.
*Why this question wins:* The MLI and BEPS-related PPT is the cutting edge of international tax law — its applicability to specific treaties is nuanced and requires checking MLI positions of both states.
*Plausible bad alternative:* Accepting that the PPT automatically applies to all DTAAs where India has ratified the MLI.
*Why bad alternative loses:* MLI modifications apply to a DTAA only if both contracting states have listed the treaty as a "Covered Tax Agreement" under the MLI and have not reserved out of the PPT — the specific positions of India and UAE under the MLI must be verified.

*Senior Advocate:* India has ratified the Multilateral Convention to Implement Tax Treaty Related Measures to Prevent BEPS (MLI) and has listed a number of DTAAs as Covered Tax Agreements. The PPT under Article 7 of the MLI is one of the minimum standards — India has adopted it. However, for the PPT to modify the India-UAE DTAA, the UAE must also be an MLI Signatory and must have listed the India-UAE DTAA as a Covered Tax Agreement. We check: the UAE has not been a signatory to the MLI as of my knowledge — the UAE has been negotiating participation but has not ratified. If the UAE has not adopted the MLI, the India-UAE DTAA is not a Covered Tax Agreement under the MLI and the PPT does not modify it. Furthermore, even if the PPT applied, it targets treaty shopping — arranging transactions to obtain treaty benefits that are contrary to the treaty's object and purpose. Our client is not a treaty shopper — he genuinely lives and works in the UAE for legitimate professional reasons; the PPT requires that one of the principal purposes of the arrangement is to obtain treaty benefits, which is not the case for a genuine UAE resident worker. The PPT argument fails on both procedural (UAE not MLI signatory) and substantive (genuine economic substance in UAE) grounds.


### case_derived_1485: Environmental Law — Coastal Regulation Zone — CRZ Notification 2019 and Development Permissions *(Two-track · Environmental · Coastal Law · National Green Tribunal)*

**Round 1**

*Junior Advocate:* Our client — a resort developer — obtained a CRZ clearance from the State Coastal Zone Management Authority (CZMA) and began construction. The National Green Tribunal has now passed an order directing stay of construction on a complaint by environmental NGOs who claim the CRZ classification of the plot is wrong. What is the CRZ regulatory framework?

*Decision dimension targeted:* Understanding the CRZ Notification 2019 framework — classification zones, permissible development, and the clearance procedure.
*Why this question wins:* CRZ law is highly technical and involves specific zone classifications with different permissibility standards — the student must know the basic framework before any challenge can be mounted.
*Plausible bad alternative:* Treating all coastal development as uniformly regulated without distinguishing CRZ zones.
*Why bad alternative loses:* CRZ zones have dramatically different permissibility regimes — CRZ-IA (Ecologically Sensitive Areas) permits almost nothing; CRZ-II (urbanised coastal areas) permits reconstruction; CRZ-III (rural coastal areas) allows tourism infrastructure — conflating them ignores the central regulatory distinction.

*Senior Advocate:* The Coastal Regulation Zone Notification 2019 (issued under the Environment Protection Act 1986) regulates development within specified distances from the High Tide Line (HTL) on the sea-coast of India. The 2019 Notification classifies coastal areas into four zones: CRZ-IA (ecologically sensitive and important areas — no-development zone); CRZ-IB (No Development Zone up to 50 metres from HTL for CRZ-I areas); CRZ-II (densely developed urban areas); CRZ-III (relatively undisturbed rural coastal areas); and CRZ-IV (water area). For our client's resort, we must first determine the correct CRZ classification of the plot as per the approved Coastal Zone Management Plan (CZMP) prepared by the State. If the NGO's complaint is that the CRZ classification is wrong, the issue is fundamentally about the CZMP — whether the plot is correctly classified in the approved CZMP. We obtain the CZMP and the CZMA's clearance record, and prepare to demonstrate that the classification and clearance were in accordance with the approved CZMP.

**Round 2**

*Junior Advocate:* The NGO argues that a mangrove patch is present on the plot which makes it CRZ-IA — a no-development zone. Our client says the "mangroves" are not true mangroves and are stray shrubs. How do we defend this technical question?

*Decision dimension targeted:* The evidentiary and procedural aspects of challenging the classification of vegetation as mangroves under CRZ regulations, and the role of expert committees.
*Why this question wins:* Mangrove identification is a technical-scientific question that courts refer to expert committees — knowing how to engage with this process is essential for the practitioner.
*Plausible bad alternative:* Producing our own expert to say the vegetation is not mangrove and claiming that settles the question.
*Why bad alternative loses:* Courts and the NGT do not accept party-appointed experts as conclusive in environmental disputes — they typically appoint an independent expert committee; proceeding as if one side's expert testimony is conclusive misunderstands the NGT's approach.

*Senior Advocate:* The question of whether the vegetation constitutes mangroves within the meaning of the CRZ Notification is a technical-scientific question. The Supreme Court in *Orissa Mining Corporation v. MoEFCC* (2013) and the NGT's consistent approach is to appoint an expert committee — typically including scientists from the Zoological Survey of India or Botanical Survey of India, the Central and State Pollution Control Boards — to examine the site and report. We should proactively request the NGT to appoint a neutral expert committee to examine whether the vegetation in question meets the botanical definition of mangroves and whether it constitutes a "mangrove patch" within the meaning of the CRZ Notification. We should avoid conducting the debate through party-appointed experts — the NGT will discount them. We produce our CZMA clearance record, which should include a site inspection report by the CZMA that addressed the vegetation — if the CZMA's own inspection found no mangroves, this is the strongest administrative record in our favour. We stay focused on the regulatory record, not just the botanical dispute.

**Round 3**

*Junior Advocate:* The NGT's stay order has been operative for two years. Can we challenge it before the Supreme Court or is there any relief mechanism within the NGT?

*Decision dimension targeted:* The appellate framework for NGT orders and the Supreme Court's supervisory jurisdiction over the NGT.
*Why this question wins:* The procedural remedies against long-running NGT stays are practically critical — the student must know the appeal route and the Supreme Court's approach to environmental stay orders.
*Plausible bad alternative:* Filing a writ petition before the High Court challenging the NGT's order.
*Why bad alternative loses:* High Courts do not have jurisdiction to interfere with NGT orders — only the Supreme Court under Article 136 has supervisory jurisdiction over the NGT; filing before the High Court is a jurisdictional error.

*Senior Advocate:* Appeals from the NGT lie directly to the Supreme Court under Section 22 of the National Green Tribunal Act 2010 — there is no intermediate appellate forum. A party aggrieved by a NGT order must approach the Supreme Court by way of a Civil Appeal or Special Leave Petition under Article 136. High Courts cannot entertain challenges to NGT orders — in *State of UP v. Amar Nath Yadav* (2014) 2 SCC 800 and several subsequent decisions, the Supreme Court has clearly delineated this jurisdictional boundary. For relief from the stay, we have three options: (a) file a miscellaneous application before the NGT itself for vacation of the stay, producing new evidence or arguing that the balance of convenience has shifted — particularly if the developer has already substantially invested; (b) seek expedited hearing before the NGT to dispose of the main matter; or (c) approach the Supreme Court under Article 136 for interim relief from the stay pending final disposal. The Supreme Court is generally reluctant to interfere with environmental stays — the precautionary principle tends to favour the NGT's conservative approach — but a two-year stay with no final hearing date is an unusual prejudice that the Supreme Court may take cognizance of.

---

### case_derived_1486: Medical Negligence — Informed Consent — Disclosure Obligation and Therapeutic Privilege *(Two-track · Consumer/Tort · Medical Law · High Court)*

**Round 1**

*Junior Advocate:* Our client underwent a surgical procedure for a benign condition. The surgeon did not disclose a 1-in-100 risk of paralysis that materialised. The client is now paralysed. The surgeon says he used the standard of care required in surgery. What is our theory of liability?

*Decision dimension targeted:* Distinguishing between the standard of care in performing surgery versus the duty to obtain informed consent — two separate bases of medical negligence.
*Why this question wins:* Informed consent negligence is doctrinally separate from procedural negligence — the student must understand that the claim can succeed even if the surgery was performed perfectly.
*Plausible bad alternative:* Arguing only that the surgical technique was negligent.
*Why bad alternative loses:* The surgery may have been performed to the highest standard of care — if the paralysis was a known risk and the patient would have refused surgery had she known, the surgeon is liable for battery or negligence in consent regardless of technical perfection.

*Senior Advocate:* The claim is in two parts. First, if we can show technical negligence in the surgical procedure — applying the *Bolam-Bolitho* test (negligence if the surgeon fell below the standard of a reasonably competent surgeon) — that is a straightforward negligence claim. Second — and more powerfully for this case — is the informed consent doctrine. The Supreme Court in *Samira Kohli v. Dr. Prabha Manchanda* (2008) 2 SCC 1 adopted the prudent patient test: the doctor must disclose all information that a reasonable patient would regard as material to her decision to undergo or refuse the procedure. A 1-in-100 risk of paralysis is a material risk — it is serious, life-altering, and any reasonable patient would want to know about it before consenting. If the paralysis was a known, disclosed risk in medical literature and the surgeon chose not to disclose it, this is a breach of the duty to obtain informed consent — independent of whether the surgery was technically flawless.

**Round 2**

*Junior Advocate:* The surgeon invokes "therapeutic privilege" — that disclosing the 1-in-100 risk of paralysis might have made the patient so anxious that she would have refused a beneficial surgery. Does therapeutic privilege justify non-disclosure?

*Decision dimension targeted:* The scope and limits of the therapeutic privilege exception to informed consent obligations and its current status in Indian law.
*Why this question wins:* Therapeutic privilege is a contested doctrine — doctors frequently invoke it and courts must carefully scrutinise whether it genuinely applies or is being used as a paternalistic shield.
*Plausible bad alternative:* Accepting that therapeutic privilege is a valid defence whenever the doctor believed disclosure would harm the patient.
*Why bad alternative loses:* Broad therapeutic privilege effectively swallows the informed consent rule — courts globally have significantly narrowed it; accepting it without scrutiny would defeat the patient's right to autonomy.

*Senior Advocate:* Therapeutic privilege allows a doctor to withhold information if disclosure would be seriously harmful to the patient — for example, if the patient has a known psychiatric condition that makes distressing information literally dangerous. It is a narrow exception. The Supreme Court in *Samira Kohli* recognised therapeutic privilege as an exception to the informed consent obligation but was clear that it cannot be invoked simply because the patient might refuse a procedure the doctor recommends. Patient autonomy — the right of a competent adult to make their own medical decisions including to refuse beneficial treatment — is a fundamental component of Article 21 dignity. Therapeutic privilege cannot be invoked paternalistically to override patient autonomy. The narrow legitimate scope is: (a) the patient has a specific known vulnerability to harmful information; (b) the information withheld was the very information that caused the harm — not general distress. Here the surgeon's justification — that the patient might refuse surgery — is precisely the paternalistic use of therapeutic privilege that courts reject. The patient had the right to refuse surgery with full information, even if that choice would be "unwise" by medical standards.

**Round 3**

*Junior Advocate:* The defendant argues that even if consent was inadequate, the paralysis would have occurred even with full disclosure because the patient would have proceeded with surgery anyway — the "but for" causation is broken. How do we address causation?

*Decision dimension targeted:* The causation test in informed consent cases — whether the "but for" test or a modified subjective-objective test applies.
*Why this question wins:* Causation in informed consent cases is doctrinally complex — the standard "but for" test may actually exculpate the surgeon in many cases; the student must know the patient-centred causation test.
*Plausible bad alternative:* Accepting the defendant's "but for" framing — that because the patient "probably would have proceeded anyway," causation fails.
*Why bad alternative loses:* If the "but for" test is applied to the hypothetical choice of a rational patient, it benefits defendants too much — courts have modified the test to ask what this patient would have decided, not what a hypothetical rational patient would do.

*Senior Advocate:* The causation question in informed consent is not straightforwardly the standard "but for" test applied to a hypothetical reasonable patient. In *Samira Kohli* the Supreme Court emphasised patient autonomy — the question is what this patient would have done had she been properly informed. This is a subjective element: if our client gives credible evidence that she would not have undergone the surgery if she had known of the 1-in-100 paralysis risk — she was risk-averse, had alternative treatments, or had expressed concerns about surgical risks — her subjective refusal would break the causation chain in the defendant's favour and complete the chain for us. We lead evidence of: (a) her subjective attitude towards risk — prior statements about preferring conservative treatment; (b) whether alternative non-surgical treatments were available that she would have chosen; (c) her post-paralysis statements about her decision had she been informed. Courts apply a modified test — the patient must satisfy the court on a balance of probabilities that she would personally have refused surgery with full information — this is subjective-objective: what would this patient have decided, assessed against what a reasonable patient in her position would consider material.


### case_derived_1487: Section 66A IT Act — Legacy — Continuing Prosecutions and Shreya Singhal's Application *(Two-track · Constitutional · Digital Rights · High Court)*

**Round 1**

*Junior Advocate:* My client is facing a criminal prosecution for a social media post under Section 66A of the IT Act 2000 — a provision declared unconstitutional by the Supreme Court in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015). The prosecution is still continuing. What is the immediate legal position?

*Decision dimension targeted:* The effect of the Supreme Court's declaration of unconstitutionality in Shreya Singhal and whether prosecutions under a void provision can continue.
*Why this question wins:* The continuing prosecution of individuals under Section 66A — even after Shreya Singhal — is a documented phenomenon; the student must know the immediate legal remedy.
*Plausible bad alternative:* Filing a fresh bail application before the Sessions Court.
*Why bad alternative loses:* The more fundamental issue is that the provision on which the prosecution rests has been declared void — the prosecution is not merely bail-eligible; it is constitutionally non-existent; a bail application does not address this root problem.

*Senior Advocate:* In *Shreya Singhal v. Union of India* (2015) 5 SCC 1, a Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court declared Section 66A of the IT Act 2000 void ab initio as violating Articles 19(1)(a) (freedom of speech) and 19(2) (reasonable restrictions). A declaration under Article 13(2) that a law is void operates from the inception — Section 66A never had legal force as far as the Constitution is concerned. Any prosecution based on Section 66A is therefore a prosecution under a non-existent provision — it has no legal foundation. The police cannot charge, the Magistrate cannot take cognizance, and no court can convict under a void provision. We file a writ petition under Article 226 before the High Court seeking quashing of the FIR, all consequential proceedings, and a direction to the police not to register any FIR under Section 66A. Alternatively, we move an application before the trial Magistrate itself, who should take judicial notice of the Supreme Court's ruling and drop the proceedings. The Supreme Court in subsequent orders has repeatedly directed states to stop registering cases under Section 66A — citing those orders strengthens our application.

**Round 2**

*Junior Advocate:* The police say they are now re-chargesheeting under Section 505 IPC (statements conducting to public mischief) — a still-valid provision — based on the same post. Can they do this?

*Decision dimension targeted:* Whether re-characterising the same facts under a constitutional provision after Section 66A is struck down constitutes an abuse of process.
*Why this question wins:* This is a sophisticated abuse-of-process question — the student must understand the limits of the State's ability to re-prosecute using different provisions for the same speech.
*Plausible bad alternative:* Accepting that the prosecution can freely switch to any available IPC provision for the same alleged act.
*Why bad alternative loses:* While the police technically can investigate under different provisions, applying a provision like Section 505 IPC — which also has free speech implications — to exactly the same speech already held protected by the Supreme Court's Shreya Singhal analysis may itself be challenged.

*Senior Advocate:* The re-characterisation of the same speech as Section 505 IPC does not automatically validate the prosecution. Section 505 IPC — "statements conducting to public mischief" — has its own constitutional validity but must be applied consistently with Article 19(1)(a) and the Shreya Singhal Court's analysis of what constitutes protected speech. The post must be evaluated afresh under Section 505's elements: did it make or publish any statement rumour or report with intent to cause or which is likely to cause fear or alarm to the public, or to any section thereof, whereby any person may be induced to commit an offence against the State or against public tranquillity? If the original post was, say, a political criticism or satire — speech that clearly has the protection of Article 19(1)(a) — re-prosecuting under Section 505 is a colorable use of the State's power to circumvent Shreya Singhal. We apply for quashing of the Section 505 charge as well: (a) the speech does not prima facie meet Section 505 ingredients; (b) the prosecution is a mala fide attempt to punish constitutionally protected speech under a different label.

**Round 3**

*Junior Advocate:* Can our client seek damages from the State for the wrongful prosecution under the unconstitutional provision?

*Decision dimension targeted:* Constitutional remedies in tort — public law compensation for prosecution under an unconstitutional law.
*Why this question wins:* The intersection of constitutional invalidity and compensatory public law remedies is an emerging and sophisticated area — the student must know the basis for claiming compensation.
*Plausible bad alternative:* Limiting the remedy to quashing the prosecution and not pursuing compensation.
*Why bad alternative loses:* The Supreme Court has developed a public law compensation remedy under Article 32/226 for violations of fundamental rights — wrongful prosecution under a void statute is a violation of Article 21 and potentially Articles 14 and 19; limiting to quashing leaves the client uncompensated for real harm suffered.

*Senior Advocate:* The Supreme Court in *Nilabati Behera v. State of Orissa* (1993) 2 SCC 746 established that constitutional courts can award compensation under Article 32/226 for violations of fundamental rights — this is a public law remedy distinct from a private law tort action. Prosecution of our client under a provision that the Supreme Court has declared void ab initio is a violation of our client's fundamental rights under Article 21 (liberty — prosecution resulted in harassment, potential custody, reputational damage), Article 19(1)(a) (the prosecution itself chilled free speech), and Article 14 (arbitrary action). We can seek constitutional damages in the writ petition: (a) compensation for the period of any custody; (b) compensation for reputational damage and professional loss; (c) expenses incurred in legal defence during the wrongful prosecution. The State will resist — arguing the prosecution was bona fide at the time. We counter: Section 66A was challenged as unconstitutional before Shreya Singhal and the prosecution should have been stayed pending that challenge; continuing prosecution under a constitutionally disputed provision was not bona fide. The quantum of compensation will be modest in public law — but the principle is available.

---

### case_derived_1488: Right to Education — Article 21A — Unaided Private Schools and 25% RTE Quota *(Two-track · Constitutional · Education Law · High Court)*

**Round 1**

*Junior Advocate:* Our client — an unaided private school — is resisting the State's direction to admit 25% economically weaker section (EWS) children in entry-level classes under Section 12(1)(c) of the RTE Act 2009. The school argues this is an unconstitutional compulsion on private property. What is the constitutional status of this obligation?

*Decision dimension targeted:* Understanding the Supreme Court's ruling in Society for Unaided Private Schools v. Union of India (2012) on Section 12(1)(c) of the RTE Act and its application to unaided private schools.
*Why this question wins:* The 25% EWS obligation is one of the most constitutionally important provisions in education law — the student must know the definitive Supreme Court ruling.
*Plausible bad alternative:* Arguing that any admission quota on a private school violates Article 19(1)(g) absolutely.
*Why bad alternative loses:* The Supreme Court has upheld Section 12(1)(c) as constitutionally valid for unaided non-minority schools — arguing absolute invalidity ignores this binding precedent.

*Senior Advocate:* In *Society for Unaided Private Schools of Rajasthan v. Union of India* (2012) 6 SCC 1, a Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court upheld Section 12(1)(c) of the RTE Act — requiring unaided non-minority private schools to admit 25% EWS/disadvantaged children in Class I — as constitutionally valid. The Court held that the right of non-minority private schools to administer their institutions under Article 19(1)(g) is subject to reasonable restrictions under Article 19(6), and the 25% quota is a reasonable restriction serving the compelling public interest of universal elementary education under Article 21A. However, the Court also held that minority schools — both aided and unaided — are protected by Article 30(1) and Section 12(1)(c) cannot be imposed on them. Our client is not a minority institution — the obligation under Section 12(1)(c) is binding. The school's recourse is ensuring proper reimbursement under Section 12(2) — the State must reimburse the per-child cost of education for EWS students up to whatever the State's per-pupil expenditure in government schools is.

**Round 2**

*Junior Advocate:* The State's reimbursement rate is much lower than the actual cost of education in our client's school. The school spends Rs. 50,000 per student per year but the State reimburses only Rs. 15,000. Is the inadequate reimbursement a ground for relief?

*Decision dimension targeted:* The legal character of the reimbursement obligation under Section 12(2) RTE Act and the remedy for inadequate reimbursement.
*Why this question wins:* Inadequate reimbursement is the most practically pressing issue for schools under the RTE Act — the student must know what Section 12(2) requires and what relief is available.
*Plausible bad alternative:* Accepting the State's reimbursement rate as government prerogative not subject to challenge.
*Why bad alternative loses:* Section 12(2) creates a statutory obligation — and the Supreme Court's upholding of Section 12(1)(c) was partly premised on the reimbursement protecting schools from undue financial burden; if the reimbursement is illusory, the constitutional balance is upset.

*Senior Advocate:* Section 12(2) of the RTE Act requires the State to reimburse per-child expenditure at a rate not exceeding the expenditure per child in government schools or the per-child fees of the school, whichever is lower. The Supreme Court's constitutional upholding of Section 12(1)(c) in *Society for Unaided Private Schools* was predicated on this reimbursement mechanism — it ensures that private schools are not required to cross-subsidise the State's constitutional obligation indefinitely. Several High Courts — including the Gujarat and Karnataka High Courts — have held that the reimbursement rate must be a genuine reimbursement, not a nominal one. If the actual cost of education is Rs. 50,000 and the State reimburses Rs. 15,000 using government school per-pupil expenditure as the ceiling, the private school effectively subsidises the State to the extent of Rs. 35,000 per child. We challenge the reimbursement rate before the High Court as inadequate — the Prescribed Authority must determine a fair reimbursement. Alternatively, we argue that if the State cannot reimburse adequately, it cannot compel the school to admit EWS students beyond its capacity to absorb the subsidy.

**Round 3**

*Junior Advocate:* A parent whose child was denied admission under the 25% EWS quota — on the ground that the school's RTE quota was "exhausted" — complains to the State. Can the parent approach the Grievance Redressal Officer and then the courts?

*Decision dimension targeted:* The enforcement mechanism for EWS students' rights under the RTE Act and the remedies available to parents when schools deny EWS admissions.
*Why this question wins:* The enforcement architecture of the RTE Act — Grievance Redressal Officer, the National Commission for Protection of Child Rights, and judicial remedies — must be understood for complete advice.
*Plausible bad alternative:* Advising the parent to directly file a writ petition against the school.
*Why bad alternative loses:* The RTE Act has a statutory grievance mechanism that must be exhausted before courts will typically entertain a writ — advising direct writ petition ignores the mandatory pre-litigation mechanism.

*Senior Advocate:* Section 32 of the RTE Act provides for a grievance redressal mechanism: a complaint may be made to a local authority or the State Government-prescribed authority. Under Section 31, there is a National Commission for Protection of Child Rights (NCPCR) mandate to monitor and enforce RTE rights, and the State Commission for Protection of Child Rights (SCPCR) at the State level plays a similar role. The parent should: (a) file a complaint before the SCPCR or the local authority designated under Section 32 for denial of admission under the RTE quota; (b) the authority can direct the school to admit the child or recommend prosecution of the school management for non-compliance under Section 13 (prohibition on capitation fee and screening procedures). If the statutory mechanism fails to provide relief, the parent can file a writ under Article 226 — courts have been willing to intervene when schools deny EWS admissions in bad faith. We also note that the school cannot claim the quota is "exhausted" if it has not actually filled 25% of its Class I seats with EWS students verified through the prescribed income/residence certificates — we verify the actual admission data before advising the client.


### case_derived_1489: Land Revenue — Mutation of Revenue Records — Effect on Title and Adverse Possession *(Two-track · Property · Revenue Law · High Court)*

**Round 1**

*Junior Advocate:* Our client purchased agricultural land and got the name mutated in the revenue records (khasra/khatauni). The original owner's legal heir now sues our client claiming the sale was void as the seller had no power to sell. Does mutation establish title?

*Decision dimension targeted:* Understanding the evidentiary value of mutation entries in revenue records and their relationship to title.
*Why this question wins:* Mutation as title is one of the most pervasive misconceptions in Indian property law — the student must know the correct position clearly.
*Plausible bad alternative:* Arguing that mutation is conclusive proof of ownership.
*Why bad alternative loses:* This is wrong in law — mutation is merely an administrative revenue record for fiscal purposes; it does not create, extinguish or confer title; asserting this would immediately undermine credibility before any court.

*Senior Advocate:* Mutation of revenue records — the process of recording a change of ownership in the khasra (field register) and khatauni (ownership register) maintained by the Revenue Department — does not confer title or establish ownership of land. The Supreme Court has consistently held in decisions including *Smt. Sawarni v. Inder Kaur* (1996) 6 SCC 223 and *Suraj Bhan v. Financial Commissioner* (2007) 6 SCC 186 that mutation entries are made for revenue purposes only — for the determination of land revenue liability — and do not affect the civil title to land. Title to immovable property in India is determined by valid registered documents under the Transfer of Property Act and the Registration Act. If the sale deed in favour of our client was registered under a valid sale by the actual owner, title passed to our client. If the seller had no title, no amount of mutation in revenue records cures the defect — our client may have bought from a non-owner and may need to defend on the basis of bona fide purchaser for value without notice if that principle assists.

**Round 2**

*Junior Advocate:* The original owner died without a will and his heirs dispute which of them had the right to sell. Our client bought from one co-sharer. Does our client get a valid title or only an interest in the share of the selling co-sharer?

*Decision dimension targeted:* The legal effect of a sale by one co-sharer of joint property on the buyer's title under Section 44 of the Transfer of Property Act.
*Why this question wins:* Co-ownership sales are extremely common and frequently misunderstood — Section 44 TPA has a specific and important rule that the student must know.
*Plausible bad alternative:* Arguing that our client acquired full ownership of the entire land because the co-sharer sold the whole property.
*Why bad alternative loses:* A co-sharer cannot alienate more than his own share — Section 44 TPA provides that a buyer from one co-sharer steps into that co-sharer's shoes as a co-owner, not as the owner of the whole; claiming full ownership is legally incorrect.

*Senior Advocate:* Section 44 of the Transfer of Property Act provides that where one of two or more co-owners transfers his share or any part thereof of the joint property, the transferee acquires the transferor's rights in the joint property to the extent of the transfer. Our client acquired only the selling co-sharer's undivided share in the agricultural land — not any greater interest. The non-selling co-sharers' interests are entirely unaffected. What our client now has is co-ownership with the other heirs. The rights of a co-owner as a transferee from another co-owner in an agricultural context may also be subject to the State's pre-emption laws — many States have statutory rights of pre-emption allowing co-sharers or neighbours to pre-empt a sale to an outsider within a specified period. We check whether the State's land revenue or tenancy legislation gives other co-sharers a right of pre-emption — if so, they may claim the transferred share from our client by paying the sale consideration within the limitation period. If pre-emption is not exercised, our client's position as co-owner of the selling heir's share is secure.

**Round 3**

*Junior Advocate:* The heir suing our client also claims adverse possession — that the heir has been in exclusive possession of the entire land for twelve years. What are the elements of adverse possession and does it defeat our client's registered title?

*Decision dimension targeted:* The elements of adverse possession under Article 65 of the Limitation Act 1963 and whether it can defeat a registered title holder who purchased before the limitation period ran.
*Why this question wins:* Adverse possession is one of the most tested doctrines in property law — the student must know the elements and particularly the Supreme Court's re-statement of the burden of proof.
*Plausible bad alternative:* Accepting that twelve years of possession conclusively extinguishes the title of the registered owner.
*Why bad alternative loses:* The Supreme Court in *Hemaji Waghaji Jat v. Bhikhabhai Khengarbhai Harijan* (2009) 16 SCC 517 re-examined adverse possession and emphasised that the possessor must clearly establish each element — nec vi, nec clam, nec precario — and the burden is heavy; twelve years alone is not sufficient if possession was not hostile.

*Senior Advocate:* For adverse possession under Article 65 of the Limitation Act 1963, the defendant (the possessor) must establish that: (a) possession was actual — physical and exclusive, not merely nominal; (b) possession was open — known to the owner, not concealed; (c) possession was hostile — adverse to the title of the true owner, not permissive or as a licensee; (d) possession was continuous — without interruption for twelve years. The Supreme Court in *Hemaji Waghaji Jat* (2009) held that the burden of proving adverse possession is on the claimant and each element must be independently established. In our case: if the heir was in possession as a legal heir following the original owner's death — possession that was believed to be rightful co-ownership — it is not "hostile" possession; it is permissive possession consistent with co-ownership rights. Mere possession by a co-heir is not adverse to the rights of other co-heirs — it is recognised tenure, not adverse tenure. The adverse possession claim should fail because the heir was not holding the land adversely to the original owner — he was holding it as heir — and possession by a co-sharer is not adverse to other co-sharers unless there is ouster and clear repudiation of the others' title, which must be demonstrated by specific acts.
